chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
title: Marching with Anderson's Buzzards band, and pay for Mardi Gras
summary: Watts played the Buzzards parade with Anderson in 1955 and 1956 and says 1963 will be his last, since the walking and playing is hard for little pay.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: In 55? Yeah, 55. I must have seen you, you know. Yeah. I used to stay with the Zulus for a while there, but this year I thought I'd change it up, you know. And I caught all of them just about the same, up there. I didn't see the Corner Club.
No, you didn't see the Corner Club.
So you've been with the Buzzards every year, huh?

Yeah, in 55, and then I was able to come back again in 56. I played for the Buzzards again with Anderson, the same trumpet player, you know Anderson, don't you? Oh, yeah, I know. Yeah, well I played with him, see, again in 55 and 56. That's why I was surprised after seven years, when I come back this Mardi Gras, that he said that two or three years ago he had changed and went and started playing for the Lions Club, see. I thought we were still going to play for the Buzzards, you know. Of course it didn't make no difference, see, because I'm out there for the Lute anyway, I ain't feel that walking no more. But I, but like I can inform you right now, I'm 56 years old, and that is the last parade. Yeah, whenever I come, be fortunate enough to come back to visit my mother and my family. See, I will get on the truck or even in the ballroom, and if I don't, if I can't be booked in either one of those places, well then I'll just take Mardi Gras off and enjoy it with my wife, but no more walking. Right. From 730 to 430, that's a little too much, and for the money. Oh. See, your money, they don't pay you nothing. I want that to be down in history, in the records. They don't pay your thing for all that walking you do and blowing on top of it. You really got to blow out there. See, you can't get by on no crutch like you can in a hall where you got a sax to pick it

See, there's three trumpets. When one takes down, the other one is blowing, the other one is blowing. And when you take a number down, you're all three blow. When you take that number out, you're all three blow.
